course_details.Overview of class:
References to the end of time—to the end of the times we live in and to the end of time itself—have become so ubiquitous nowadays and so casual as to be almost banal. Yet they point towards something real. Suddenly, we are living in the subjunctive. Allusions to the future are hedged with contingency and uncertainty.

The question for this course is not how ought people live in this time, but how are they living. How are humans in their relations with each other and with non-humans making their way through a such a deeply disturbing and dangerous period in human history, when the horizon of the future itself seems to be vanishing? How does living in this time shape decisions? What becomes of memory and hope? How are humans to live responsibly and lovingly in this context?

We ask these questions in relation to the climate crisis; the development of AI; the decline of democracies and rise of religious authoritarianism around the globe, and other challenges. At the very end of the course, we will think critically and deeply about the possibilities for hope.

As a course in the humanities, we will be concerned with the questions traditionally taken up by the disciplines organized under this heading. How do we read in this time? How do we create? What becomes of the human imagination when the horizon of the future is so clouded?

course_details.Overview of class: One of the largest and most ancient of all religions, Hinduism comprises a family of related traditions. Over the last 5000 years, the Hindu traditions of South Asia have developed a remarkable diversity of rituals, beliefs, and spiritual practices and a pantheon of hundreds and thousands of gods and goddesses, from the elephant headed Ganeṣa to the fierce goddess Kālī as well as many local deities. This course will examine the breadth of the Hindu traditions as they have developed over time, highlighting the major elements that characterize them collectively, such as ritual sacrifice (yajña), world renunciation (saṃnyāsa), law (dharma), spiritual discipline (yoga), devotion (bhakti), worship (pūjā), and theology. During the course we will explore both the scriptures of Hinduism as well as its practices. We will pay particular attention to how these traditions have contributed to the development of modern Hinduism.
course_details.Learning Objectives:

3) be able to interpret primary and secondary sources critically and with imagination
4) be able to demonstrate familiarity with the methods and priorities of the academic study of religion

course_details.Overview of class: This course provides an introduction to key aspects of the Buddha's life stories, his teachings, and Buddhist traditions in Asia and beyond. Through a careful examination of Buddhist history and the literature produced within these traditions, we will explore key teachings and concepts, including the Four Noble Truths, the Two Truths, impermanence, suffering, no-self, the Middle Way, karma, merit, rebirth, nirvana, and enlightenment. Drawing on these concepts, we will seek to understand the moral values, philosophical insights, ritual practices, and social concerns that have shaped Buddhism over centuries of dynamic change across diverse cultural contexts. More specifically, we examine the historical development of Buddhist teachings along three major traditions, Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana, as well as contemporary Buddhist practices. In the contemporary context, particular attention will be given to the global significance of mindfulness and ongoing dialogues between Buddhism and science, ecology, and visual culture.

course_details.Overview of class: In this course students will be introduced to the variety of Black religions in the United States from the early 19th century to the present. course_details.Overview of class:
Some say America is currently undergoing a process of "Buddhification," meaning that Buddhism is cropping up everywhere, even in places one would least expect. Tech industry billionaires tout Buddhist mindfulness techniques at the annual Wisdom 2.0 conference, and Google offers mindfulness training courses taught by a Zen abbot. Mindfulness is also being presented as a panacea for those suffering from physical and mental pain, readily available in American hospital settings and psychological counseling services. Buddha images too can be found far from Buddhist temples—at the hip restaurant Buddha-Bar located in many cities around the world one can sip cocktails and dine before a massive Buddha statue while listening to lounge music. And in the Chicago area, one encounters Buddha head sculptures positioned on the ground in parks, by roads, and even in public school playgrounds as part of the Ten Thousand Ripples art project.

How, and why, did aspects of Buddhism enter all of these different social locations? Why does Buddhism receive a pass more often than other religions by the "spiritual but not religious" crowd? Can Buddhism be secular? In what ways is Buddhism compatible with science, and can Buddhist practices be proven effective using scientific methods? Can paying better attention by means of Buddhist meditation practices liberate us from suffering caused by digital distraction? In what ways can Buddhist articulations of interdependence, no self, and compassion be resources for addressing racial and structural injustice, even as sexual abuse, racism, and trans/homophobia continue to traumatize members of some Buddhist communities? These are some of the many questions we will consider through readings by some of the most creative Buddhist leaders, critics, and consumers of our time.

The course counts toward Religion, Health and Medicine (RHM) religious studies major concentration.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Recognize the key features of modern Buddhism
• Reflect on Buddhism and race, with a focus on articulations of Asian and Black Buddhist experiences and embodiment • Critically assess the ways in which Buddhist ideas & images are used in contemporary information sources such as websites, apps, TV/film, YouTube, and so forth
• Evaluate the benefits and the costs of the widespread application of Buddhist mindfulness techniques to secular pursuits, in particular in the contexts of business and medicine
• Consider the ways in which Buddhist conceptions are contributing to social justice and environmentalism • Gain confidence in speaking through active participation in class and in research and analytical writing through writing assignments

course_details.Topic: Queerness, Spirits, and Ghosts: Buddhism in Southe
course_details.Overview of class:
Queerness, Spirits, and Ghosts: Lived Buddhism in Southeast Asia:

This course, "Queerness, Spirits, and Ghosts: Lived Buddhism in Southeast Asia," explores how Buddhist deities and ghosts animate everyday religious life and practices of devotion in contemporary Southeast Asia. From fear and anguish to safety and calm, Buddhist deities and ghosts inspire a range of emotions in devotees who turn to them for help— when they are suffering from illness, seeking protection from war, undergoing financial challenges, and more. These more-than-human beings, from the Thai ghost Mae Nak to the Burmese Buddhist wizard Bo Min Gaung, create physical and emotional bonds with humans, together constituting a cosmos filled with human and beyond-human presence.

Taking a lived religion approach, we will study how ordinary religious people practice a Buddhism that remains tethered to the spirit world even as state governments ban religious practices related to these spirits. We will also investigate major 18th-21st century religious modernization efforts, when colonial powers aimed to replace indigenous and supernatural beliefs in ghosts and deities with a purely rational and human-centered Buddhism (now singularly focused on the Buddha), situating these religious transformations in broader contexts of European colonialism throughout mainland Southeast Asia.

We will study how these religious modernization efforts transformed local conceptions of Buddhism while failing to rid Thai, Cambodian, Lao, and Burmese people of their relationships with spirits and ghosts. Foregrounding ethnographic studies and queer and trans Thai contemporary film (where queer people often become ghosts after death), we will investigate how living religious practitioners continue to exist in intimate relationships with the more-than-human realm as they make offerings of fresh flower garlands, red Fanta soda, lipstick, money, and more to the ghosts who provoke fear and the deities who offer them protection.

The course counts toward Religion, Law and Politics (RLP) and Religion, Sexuality and Gender (RSG) religious studies major concentrations.

course_details.Overview of class:
The Talmud is one of the most important works of Jewish literature. For the last millennium, Talmud study has been a central part of Jewish religious and cultural practice. Despite the splintering of Judaism into different denominations, Jews the world over are unified by their commitment to studying Talmud. The Talmud is an unusual work of literature, and it has been credited as an influence on codes of law, sermons, modern works of Jewish literature, and even Seinfeld. This course will explain the Talmud's import and durability within Jewish culture while introducing students to the rigors of legal analysis that lie at the heart of most talmudic passages. The course is ideal for those interested in religion, law, logic games and questions of textual interpretation. The course will study the Talmud entirely in English translation; there is neither a language prerequisite nor an expectation of prior experience reading the Talmud.

The course counts toward Religion, Law and Politics (RLP) religious studies major concentration.

course_details.Overview of class:
Today, Eastern Christianity is far outnumbered by Catholicism and Protestantism, yet in the Middle Ages Eastern Christians made up a majority of the Christian world. From the fourth century to the thirteenth, the Byzantine Empire brought Orthodoxy to the Caucasus, Ethiopia, Nubia, and Eastern Europe, while the Syriac Christians who had broken away from Constantinople carried out an immense program of evangelization across Iran, Central Asia, India, and China. The Eastern Christian missionaries carried their teaching to these distant lands, overcoming extraordinary obstacles and at times risking their lives. Who were they? How did they travel such vast distances? What did they bring with them? How did they find a common language, both literally and figuratively, with the local population? By what means did they win the favor of local elites? How did they manage to prevail over deeply rooted beliefs?


1. What is a religious mission? The history of the term and the emergence of the concept itself.
2. Was there missionary activity in Buddhism, Manichaeism, Zoroastrianism, and Islam?
3. Christianity as a missionary religion. What does "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations." mean? Who were the apostles?
4. Christian proselytism within the pagan Roman Empire. When did the new religion move beyond the imperial borders? Did the apostle Thomas ever visit India?
5. The transformation of Christianity into the state religion of the Empire and the reinterpretation of mission as a form of imperial expansion.
6. Who Christianized Armenia, Georgia, and Caucasian Albania? Greeks and Syrians in the Caucasus.
7. The arrival of missionaries in Ethiopia: who were the "Nine Saints"? Edesius and Frumentius: real people or symbols?
8. How did Constantinople baptize the "barbarians"? After the baptism, did the cease to be "barbarians" in the eyes of the Byzantines?
9. The conversion of Nubia: the state Church and the "heretical" Church as rivals in the mission field.
10. The Eastern Christian Churches: ‘Nestorians' and Miaphysites as missionaries, and their strengths and disadvantages compared to the Church of Constantinople.
11. Syriac missionaries in Central Asia, Tibet, and China. The Buddhist reinterpretation of Christianity.
12. Cyril and Methodius, Byzantine missionaries among the Western Slavs: their triumph and catastrophe.
13. Byzantine and Western Christian missionaries competing for Bulgaria and Hungary. Why did the religious destinies of Serbia and Croatia diverge?
14. Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos and his emissaries in the North Caucasus: a shift in the Empire's missionary paradigm.
15. The baptism of Rus': how many stages? A revolution from above or a gradual percolation from below? Is the sensational claim about the Novgorod Psalter credible?
16. The strange fate of Orthodoxy in Lithuania. Old Rus' as a secondary missionary center: the Karelians, Saams and the Volga Bulgars.
17. Syriac missionaries among the Mongols: the Christianity of the Great Khans.
18. The rise of Islam and the gradual displacement of the Eastern Churches. The last attempts at Byzantine missionary work.
19. Missions initiated by the Muscovite Tsardom and the Russian Empire.
20. Why did missionaries so often succeed, and when did they meet with defeat?

course_details.Overview of class:
Islamic law - the sacred law of Islam grounded in the Qur'an, the practice of the Prophet Muhammad, and the writings of Muslim scholars and jurists - stretches back nearly 1400 years. This course offers, first, an overview of the origins and evolution of Islamic law from the life of Muhammad to end of the classical era. We then seek, secondly, to understand how colonialism and the modern nation-state affected the conceptualization and implementation of Islamic law in the modern period. To these ends, we look in-depth at two specific areas of law - marriage and divorce, and criminal law - in two specific regions: the Ottoman empire and contemporary Iran.​

course_info.course_name: Religion, Violence, and Nonviolence in the US

course_details.Topic: Religion, Violence, and Nonviolence in the US
course_details.Overview of class:
Many today argue that religion is inherently violent-the cause of national rivalries and wars, the justification for hierarchies and abuses, etc. At the same time, many also argue that violence is antithetical to "true" religion and is actually an outgrowth of human imperfections imposed on the divine. This course takes a different tack, identifying violence and religion as important aspects of human cultures without a given, natural, or immutable relationship to each other. We track how religious Americans have thought about, used, and avoided violence. We explore key moments in US history where violence, nonviolence, and religion came together, broke apart, refracted, and realigned. We think capaciously about the forms violence takes-from colonialism to war to enslavement to racism to hunting and eating-and resist painting religion with a single brush. Students in this course will draw upon the knowledge, wisdom, theories, and methods of the humanities and interpretive social sciences to craft cogent and compelling arguments to understand and explain how religion, violence, and nonviolence have brought us to where we are today.

The course counts toward Religion, Law and Politics (RLP) religious studies major concentration.
course_details.Learning Objectives: To develop complex understandings of the relationships among religion, violence, and nonviolence. To sample ways these themes have manifested in US history and culture. To gain facility with interdisciplinary scholarship and strengthen argumentation and academic writing.

course_details.Overview of class:
Death: Myth and Meaning - The Borderlands of Life and Death around the World:
This course explores global perspectives on the ways human beings have made and continue to make sense of death, dying, and the afterlife. Making sense of death often includes the presence of more-than-human entities who are involved in and around human life, death, and dying such as spirits, ghosts, the undead and the gods. Readings and discussions will consider the ramifications of death and dying not only in our (human) world, but how such phenomena ripple out into other worlds unfamiliar and strange to us such as the spirit world, the animal world, and worlds beyond our world. Death and dying creates a slippage between these worlds so that the borders between them are crossed and re-crossed by humans and non-humans until such borders become blurred and ineffectual. We will engage with this blurriness, considering borders both physical and spectral, through wide-ranging readings from the fields of religious studies, anthropology, history, critical theory, literature, poetry, and theology. We will also weigh the long-standing human preoccupation with "good death." By and large, human beings have viewed "good death" as deaths that occur in old age, that are not violent, that occur while an individual is in "good standing" in their particular religious tradition, and that do not create any unwanted spiritual or spectral residue in the form of unruly ghosts, spirits, monsters, or walking undead. However, because so very few deaths fit these criteria, the question must be raised - does "good death" as conceived of by humans even exist?

The course counts toward Religion, Health and Medicine (RHM) religious studies major concentration.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will know a variety of global perspectives on death, dying, and dead bodies and how those perspectives engage with more-than or other-than-human entities such as spirits of various types, ghosts, the walking undead, the gods, etc. Students will understand how peoples from around the world have made and continue to make sense of the phenomena of death, dying, and the afterlife as well as the perceived presence of the more-than/other-than-human in the world. Additionally, students will understand how people across the world wrestle with and articulate the idea of a "good death." Students will understand how the global perspectives discussed in class consider the ramifications of "good" and "bad" deaths upon our world and other worlds such as the spirit world and the animal world. By engaging with texts from a variety of scholarly disciplines, students will practice interdisciplinary scholarship and know how scholars from different disciplines engage with the topics of the course. Students will also know how to form rigorous and creative arguments and analyses. Lastly, students will know how to hold perspectives from people who are different from themselves, who exist across the world and across time.

course_details.Overview of class:
This seminar is an inquiry into how we experience religion in the world today. It takes seriously the idea of religion as mediated phenomena. We experience the religious through an engagement with multiple sensorial forms—things seen, felt, tasted, heard, and smelt. These can include a wide set of media ranging from YouTube videos of preachers to calendars with images of Hindu deities sold in bazars; mechanized prayer counters to the corporeal remains of venerated figures; food distributed in Hindu temples, Muslim shrines, Christian churches and Sikh gurdwaras to water brought back from pilgrimage to holy sites; Gregorian chants to Muslim calls to prayer; incense lit to commemorate the dead to camphor burnt before the image of the divine. The spaces in which we experience these religious phenomena are ever broadening as well. We do not experience the religious in places of worship alone but also at museums and in public buildings, on superhighways and in cyberspace.

Counts toward the Media, Technology, Journalism and Religion (MTJR) religious studies major concentration.

While this seminar adopts the perspective of religious materiality, with its concern for aesthetics, presence, memory, and space, it does not require previous knowledge of specific theories or familiarity with any particular religious tradition. It invites students specializing in different traditions and frameworks to engage with scholarship on religion and media in the hope that it offers a fresh perspective on their own materials.

course_details.Overview of class:
Secularities: Thinking with, through, and against "Religion":

This course will introduce students to a range of approaches to theorizing the category of "religion" in recent interdisciplinary scholarship. In this course, these approaches will revolve primary around theories of secularity - that is, theories of how the category of "religion" is produced, negotiated, maintained, and/or contested in its intersections with other domains of human life against which it is often defined, e.g. "culture," "society," "economy," and so on. We will also see some of the ways scholars have approached the ways that the category of religion informs, intersects with, and/or is constitutive of law and politics. We will begin with pioneering work in this subject from Talal Asad, Winnifred Sullivan, and Saba Mahmoud. We will then proceed to explore how a second wave of scholars on secularity put these foundational texts in conversation with a range of archives, drawing on scholars such as Elizabeth Hurd and Mayanthi Fernando. Finally, we turn our attention to the most recent scholarship in this vein from the likes of J. Barton Scott, Joseph Blankholm, Elayne Oliphant, and Charles McCrary.
